text: Day three. Two fourteen in the morning. You've just locked the doors of the supermarket you work in.
Outside, the parking lot is full. Nobody out there is shopping.
Kai... are they gonna get in?
Not if we stay quiet. Turn off the light.
Three days ago, this was a normal Tuesday. Now the whole country is falling apart.
What if a zombie virus started in the United States?
Day one. Seven a.m. You just got home from your night shift. Your mom is leaving for hers.
There's pancakes in the fridge. Mira's bus is at eight. Don't let her take that walkie-talkie to school.
It's for emergencies!
Kai. If anything ever happens, you look after your sister. Promise me.
Mom, nothing's gonna happen. It's Tuesday.
On the TV behind her, nobody is paying attention to a tiny story from West Texas.
It doesn't start in a lab. It starts in a barn, with a bat.
A rancher tries to move it off a beam.|It bites his hand.|A tiny bite.|He wraps it and forgets about it.
Here's the thing. Something like this already exists.
Rabies travels along your nerves, all the way up to your brain.|It makes animals aggressive.|It makes them want to bite.|And once the symptoms start, it's almost always fatal.
Rabies is slow. It takes weeks. This one takes six hours.
And that afternoon, the rancher gets on a plane.
His connection is in Atlanta. The busiest airport on the planet.
Atlanta's airport handles more than a hundred million passengers a year.|That's almost three hundred thousand people every single day.
When he lands, he's burning with fever, confused... and angry.
At gate B twelve, he bites a security guard.|The guard finishes his shift and goes home to his family.
And the three hundred passengers who walked past them are now flying to forty different cities.
Here's what makes zombies so scary. Not the teeth. The math.
In two thousand nine, mathematicians in Canada actually modelled a zombie outbreak.|Their result: unless the response is fast and hard, zombies win.|Every single time.
One infected person bites two.|Those two bite four.|After ten rounds, that's a thousand people.|After twenty, it's a million.
Eleven p.m. You're stocking cereal when your phone starts buzzing. And it doesn't stop.
Attacks at the airport? That's fifteen minutes from here.
Kai, listen to me. Don't come to the hospital. Whatever happens, do not come here.
Mom? Mom, what's going on?
Get Mira in the morning. Stay together. I love you, okay? I have to go.
The line goes dead. That's the last time you hear her voice.
Day two. You run home and grab Mira. Every phone in the city screams at the same time.
Where's Mom?
She's at work. She's fine. She'll call. Come on.
And everybody has the same idea: get in the car and get out.

When Hurricane Rita threatened Texas in two thousand five, around three million people tried to evacuate at once.|The traffic jam stretched for over a hundred miles.|Cars ran out of gas on the highway.
A highway full of stuck cars is the worst place to be.|You can't drive.|You can't run.|You can't hide.
So you do the opposite. You walk back to the one place with food, water, and steel shutters.
Kai! Thank God. Get inside, quick. Who's this?
My sister, Mira. Mira, this is Mr. Ruiz. My boss.
Not anymore, kid. Today we're just neighbours.
A supermarket sounds like the perfect hideout. But stores don't actually store very much.
Most supermarkets get deliveries almost every day.|If the trucks stop, the shelves are empty in about three days.
Except nobody else is coming here. They're all stuck on the highway.
Which brings you back to two fourteen a.m. And the hand on the glass.
Day five. You start watching them from the roof. And you learn the rules.
Rule one: they hunt by sound.|One can on a car roof, and every head on the street turns.
Rule two: they don't climb. Stairs, ladders, the roof. You're safe up high.
Rule three: never go anywhere alone.
Survival experts use the rule of threes.|You can last about three minutes without air, three days without water, and three weeks without food.|Water is what you protect first.
Two hundred bottles. Four people. We're good for a month.
Four?
Somebody's knocking on the back door.
Please! I'm not bitten! I'm a paramedic!
Everybody says that.
She came in daylight. She's alone. Let's check her arms first.
Opening that door could save a life. Or end four.
You check her arms, her neck, her hands. Nothing.
Thank you. You have no idea what it's like out there.
It's in the brain.|The part that makes you afraid shuts off.|The part that makes you angry goes to full volume.
That sounds like fiction. But nature already does it.
There's a fungus in the rainforest that takes over an ant's body.|It makes the ant climb a plant, bite down, and wait.|Then it grows out of its head.
And a tiny parasite called Toxoplasma makes infected rats lose their fear of cats.|They walk right up to them.
Can Mom get it?
Your mom works in a hospital, sweetie. Hospitals have plans. She's probably safer than all of us.
Dana doesn't tell you what she saw at the hospital. And you don't ask.
Day fourteen. The power is gone. The phones are dead. But radio doesn't need cell towers.
At night, AM radio waves bounce off the upper atmosphere.|A station hundreds of miles away can suddenly come through clearly.
This is Sergeant Holt, U.S.|Army.|A safe zone has been established in Montana.|Repeat, Montana.|Travel north.|Avoid all cities.
And the military really did plan for this.|In two thousand eleven, the Pentagon wrote a training plan called CONPLAN eight eight eight eight.|A plan for zombies.
Scientists at Cornell University simulated a zombie outbreak across America.|The cities fall first.|The safest place is the empty northern Rocky Mountains.
Montana is two thousand miles away.
Then we need a vehicle that isn't stuck on the highway.
There's one. The delivery truck in the parking lot. Full tank. Forty metres away.
Day twenty-one. Moonless night. You move in a line. Nobody makes a sound.
Then Mira's walkie-talkie switches on.
Run! Run!
Go, go, go! Get in!
You make it. All four of you. But Mr. Ruiz is holding his arm.
It's nothing. Just a scratch.
Kai... We need to talk.
I know, kid. I know. Take care of your sister. Drive north and don't stop.
At the next crossroads, he gets out. He doesn't look back. You don't either. You can't.
It was my fault.
Hey. No. It wasn't. He chose to save us. Okay?
Nine days. Two thousand miles. You avoid every city. You sleep in the truck, one person always awake.
New York City packs about twenty-nine thousand people into every square mile. Montana has fewer than eight.
And that's the secret.|A virus that spreads by biting needs people close together.|Out here, there's nobody to bite.
The further north you drive, the colder it gets. And the infected get slower.
Day thirty. A fence. Floodlights. Soldiers.
Sleeves up. Both arms. Let me see your necks... You're clean. Welcome to Montana.
Out of three hundred and thirty million Americans, only a few hundred thousand made it here.
The virus wasn't stopped by soldiers. It was stopped by cold, by distance, and by empty land.
Kai! The board! Look! It's Mom!
Arrived day twelve. Tent forty-eight.
Tent forty-eight is empty. Her badge is on the bed. Next to it, a notebook.
On the last page, in your mom's handwriting, four words.
The bat wasn't an accident.
Would you have opened the door for Dana?|Tell us in the comments.|And subscribe, so you don't miss part two.
